☛ What is the main objective of this amendment? → Promoting gender inclusivity
☛ Was the Central Waqf Council abolished? → No
☛ Were Waqf properties exempted from legal scrutiny? → No
☛ Is there any provision for privatisation of Waqf properties? → No

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (12/06/2025) Shift 2
q: Which of the following was the final court of appeal for India under British rule?
qs.e: During British rule, the highest appellate authority in India's judicial system was the Privy Council located in London. From 1726 to 1949, the Privy Council served as the final court of appeal for Indian cases. It was an advisory body to the British monarch and held supreme judicial authority in civil and criminal matters. Appeals were heard against decisions of the High Courts of Calcutta, Bombay, and Madras. The Government of India Act 1935 established a Judicial Committee for Indian matters. After India's independence in 1947, the jurisdiction of the Privy Council was terminated in 1949 when the Federal Court became the highest court, later replaced by the Supreme Court in 1950.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the Privy Council established? → 1726
☛ When did the Privy Council's jurisdiction over India end? → 1949
☛ Which act created the Federal Court of India? → Government of India Act 1935
☛ Which act constituted the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council for India? → Government of India Act 1935
☛ When did the Federal Court of India come into existence? → 1937

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (12/06/2025) Shift 2
q: When were the Municipal Corporations of Calcutta and Bombay established?
qs.e: The Municipal Corporations of Calcutta (Kolkata) and Bombay (Mumbai) were established in the year 1726. These are among the oldest municipal corporations in India, established during the rule of the British East India Company. The Charter of 1726 (Mayor's Court Act) was issued, which laid the foundation for municipal corporations in Calcutta, Bombay, and Madras. Later, in 1882, Lord Ripon's tenure saw reforms to strengthen local self-government. The Government of India Act of 1919 gave more powers to municipal corporations, but the establishment year remains 1726. It is important to note that the Madras Municipal Corporation was also established in 1687, making it the oldest, but for Calcutta and Bombay, the correct year is 1726.
qs.kf:
☛ Oldest Municipal Corporation in India → Madras (1687)
☛ Establishment of Calcutta Municipal Corporation → 1726
☛ Establishment of Bombay Municipal Corporation → 1726
☛ Mayor's Court Act year → 1726
☛ Lord Ripon's local self-government reforms → 1882

q: The name of the newest Antarctica research base commissioned in 2015 is
qs.e: India's third Antarctic research station 'Bharati' was commissioned in 2015. It is located in the Larsemann Hills region at an altitude of 55 meters above sea level. The station was built using 140 containers and can accommodate 47 personnel. It is used for biological, geological, and climate research. The first station 'Dakshin Gangotri' was established in 1983 but abandoned in 1989. The second station 'Maitri' was set up in 1989 and is still operational. 'Bharati' is equipped with advanced facilities and strengthens India's participation in scientific studies under the Antarctic Treaty.
qs.kf:
☛ India's first Antarctic station → Dakshin Gangotri (1983)
☛ India's second Antarctic station → Maitri (1989)
☛ India's third Antarctic station → Bharati (2015)
☛ Bharati station is located in → Larsemann Hills, Antarctica
☛ Bharati station built using how many containers → 140 containers

q: Parliament House in Delhi was constructed during
qs.e: The Parliament House (old building) in Delhi was constructed between 1921 and 1927. It was designed by British architects Sir Edwin Lutyens and Herbert Baker. The building was part of the development of New Delhi after the capital was shifted from Kolkata to Delhi in 1911. It was inaugurated in 1927 and served as the home of the Indian Parliament. Even after the inauguration of the new Parliament building in 2023, the old building remains historically significant.
qs.kf:
☛ Who designed the old Parliament House? → Sir Edwin Lutyens and Herbert Baker
☛ When was the new Parliament building inaugurated? → 2023
☛ When did Delhi become the capital of India? → 1911
☛ What is the current name of the Parliament House? → Parliament House (Old)
☛ Other major building designed by Lutyens? → Rashtrapati Bhavan

q: While watching 3D movies at the theatre, we have to wear special glasses because?
o: The glasses allow our left and right eyes to see different images
3-D movies use special colors which cannot be sensed by the human eye
3-D movies are brighter than ordinary movies and can hurt our eyes if seen directly
The glasses allow both the eyes to see similar images
qs.e: 3D movies use a technique called stereoscopic imaging, where two slightly different images of the same scene are projected simultaneously - one for the left eye and one for the right eye. These images are captured from angles that mimic the natural distance between our eyes (interpupillary distance). Special glasses, with polarized lenses or red-cyan anaglyph filters, ensure each eye sees only its intended image. The brain then combines these two distinct 2D images to create the perception of depth and a three-dimensional (3D) effect. Without the glasses, both images overlap, resulting in a blurry and confusing view. Thus, the glasses are essential for separating the images and enabling the 3D experience.
qs.kf:
☛ What technique is used in 3D movies? → Stereoscopic imaging
☛ Why are two images used in 3D films? → To create depth and 3D effect
☛ What type of lenses are used in 3D glasses? → Polarized or red-cyan lenses
☛ What is the distance between human eyes called? → Interpupillary distance
☛ How does a 3D screen appear without glasses? → Blurry and confusing

q: Name India's first Superfast train.
qs.e: India's first Superfast train is the Deccan Queen, which was started on 1 June 1930. This train runs between Mumbai and Pune and reaches speeds of up to 120 km/h. The Deccan Queen holds an important place in Indian Railways history as it was the country's first high-speed train. Shatabdi, Duronto, and Rajdhani Express were introduced later. The Deccan Queen is still operational and known for its quality service.
qs.kf:
☛ India's first Superfast train → Deccan Queen
☛ Deccan Queen started on → 1 June 1930
☛ Route of Deccan Queen → Mumbai-Pune
☛ First Rajdhani Express → Started in 1969
☛ First Shatabdi Express → Started in 1988

q: When did the RTI Act come into effect?
qs.e: The Right to Information (RTI) Act is a landmark law in India that empowers citizens to access government information. It was passed by Parliament on June 15, 2005, and came into full effect on October 12, 2005. The act aims to promote transparency and accountability in governance. By enabling citizens to request information from public authorities, it helps reduce corruption and strengthens democracy. The RTI Act applies to all states and union territories, with natural persons having the right to request information. It also mandates public authorities to proactively disclose certain information. The act has been instrumental in exposing corruption and inefficiencies in various government departments.
qs.kf:
☛ When was RTI Act passed? → 15 June 2005
☛ When did RTI Act come into effect? → 12 October 2005
☛ What is the objective of RTI Act? → Transparency and accountability
☛ In which year did RTI Act come into force? → 2005
☛ Which right is related to RTI in the Indian Constitution? → Article 19(1)(a)

q: How many schedules are there in the Wildlife Protection Act, 1972 of India?
qs.e: The Wildlife Protection Act, 1972 of India contains four schedules. These schedules provide varying degrees of protection to different species. Schedule I includes endangered species that receive absolute protection. Schedule II includes specially protected animals whose hunting is prohibited but may be allowed under certain conditions. Schedule III and IV include less protected species with regulated hunting. The Act originally had 6 schedules, but amendments reduced it to 4 schedules currently in force. The schedules classify species based on the level of protection required, with Schedule I offering the highest level of protection.
qs.kf:
☛ How many schedules are in the Wildlife Protection Act, 1972? → 4
☛ What type of species are included in Schedule I? → Endangered species
☛ Which schedule provides absolute protection? → Schedule I
☛ What is the provision of Schedule II? → Specially protected animals
☛ What do Schedule III and IV contain? → Less protected species

q: 2 October 2019 marks the________________ birth anniversary of Mahatma Gandhi.
qs.e: Mahatma Gandhi was born on 2 October 1869. Therefore, 2 October 2019 marked his 150th birth anniversary. Gandhi was a prominent leader of India's freedom struggle and advocated non-violence and truth. He is revered as the Father of the Nation in India. His birthday is also celebrated as the International Day of Non-Violence.
qs.kf:
☛ When was Mahatma Gandhi born? → 2 October 1869
☛ Who called Gandhi 'Father of the Nation'? → Subhas Chandra Bose
☛ When is International Day of Non-Violence observed? → 2 October
☛ Which movement was started by Gandhi in 1920? → Non-Cooperation Movement
☛ When was Gandhi assassinated? → 30 January 1948

q: After the signing of which treaty did the European Community come to be known as the European Union?
qs.e: The Treaty of Maastricht, also known as the Treaty on European Union, was signed on 7 February 1992 and came into force on 1 November 1993. It transformed the European Economic Community (EEC) into the European Union (EU). The treaty established the three-pillar structure: the European Communities, Common Foreign and Security Policy, and Justice and Home Affairs. It laid the groundwork for the euro currency and introduced the concept of EU citizenship. The treaty also increased the powers of the European Parliament.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the Maastricht Treaty signed? → 7 February 1992
☛ When did the Maastricht Treaty take effect? → 1 November 1993
☛ What are the symbols of the European Union? → Euro currency, European flag, and anthem
☛ How many member countries does the EU have currently? → 27 (as of 2024)
☛ Which treaty established the European Economic Community? → Treaty of Rome, 1957

q: In which year did the Government of India pass the Water (Prevention and Control Pollution) Act to safeguard our water resources?
qs.e: The Government of India passed the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act in the year 1974 to safeguard water resources. This act provides a comprehensive legal framework for the prevention and control of water pollution. It led to the establishment of the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) and State Pollution Control Boards (SPCBs). The act regulates the discharge of pollutants from industrial and domestic sources into water bodies. Its objective is to maintain water quality and protect aquatic life. This act was later amended in 1988.
qs.kf:
☛ Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act passed → 1974
☛ Central body established under this act → CPCB
☛ Year of CPCB establishment → 1974
☛ Amendment year of this act → 1988
☛ Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act passed → 1981

q: The best-known pastoral and hunter-gatherer tribes, the 'Mongols', inhabited ____________.
qs.e: The Mongols are renowned as a pastoral and hunter-gatherer tribe that historically inhabited the vast steppes and grasslands of Central Asia. This region includes parts of modern-day Mongolia, Russia, Kazakhstan, and China. Under Genghis Khan in the 13th century, the Mongols established the largest contiguous land empire in history. Their lifestyle was heavily reliant on herding livestock and hunting, which were perfectly suited to the arid and semi-arid grasslands of Central Asia. Other options such as the Arabian Peninsula, South Asia, or South-East Asia are not the original homeland of the Mongols. The Mongols' nomadic culture and military prowess shaped much of Eurasian history.
qs.kf:
☛ Original homeland of Mongols → Central Asia
☛ Founder of Mongol Empire → Genghis Khan
☛ Primary economic activity of Mongols → Pastoralism and hunting
☛ Period of Mongol Empire expansion → 13th-14th century
☛ Major dynasty established by Mongols in China → Yuan Dynasty

q: Which party formed the government in the state of Panjab in Provincial election of 1937 under British-India rule?
qs.e: The 1937 provincial elections were held under the Government of India Act 1935. In Punjab, the Unionist Party formed the government under the leadership of Sir Sikander Hayat Khan. The party primarily represented landlords and peasants and included Muslims, Hindus, and Sikhs. The Congress and Muslim League failed to gain majority in Punjab. The Unionist Party was founded in 1923.
qs.kf:
☛ 1937 Provincial Elections → Held under Government of India Act 1935
☛ Party that formed government in Punjab → Unionist Party
☛ Leader of Unionist Party → Sir Sikander Hayat Khan
☛ Communities in the party → Muslims, Hindus, Sikhs
☛ Unionist Party founded → 1923

q: Which of the following political parties is NOT in alliance with Maha Vikas Aghadi (English ∶ Maharashtra Development Front) Government?
qs.e: The Maha Vikas Aghadi (MVA) was formed in November 2019 in Maharashtra. It consists of three main parties: Shiv Sena, Nationalist Congress Party (NCP), and Indian National Congress. The alliance was created after Shiv Sena broke its alliance with BJP to form the government. Janata Dal (United) is primarily active in Bihar and is currently part of the National Democratic Alliance (NDA). It has no significant presence in Maharashtra and is not a constituent of MVA.
qs.kf:
☛ When was MVA formed? → November 2019
☛ Which parties are part of MVA? → Shiv Sena, NCP, Congress
☛ What was the main objective of MVA? → To form government in Maharashtra as an alternative to BJP
☛ Who is the leader of JD(U)? → Nitish Kumar
☛ Which alliance is JD(U) part of? → NDA

q: First of the major environmental protection act to be promulgated in India was-
qs.e: The first major environmental protection act to be promulgated in India was the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974. This act was enacted to prevent and control water pollution. It led to the establishment of the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) and State Pollution Control Boards. Subsequently, the Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981 and the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 were enacted. The Noise Pollution Rules were notified in 2000. This act was passed under Article 253 of the Constitution to implement international conventions like the Stockholm Conference, 1972.

☛ Under which article was the Water Act enacted? → Article 253
☛ Under which act was CPCB established? → Water Act, 1974
☛ When was the Stockholm Conference held? → 1972
☛ When was the Air Act enacted? → 1981

q: Which is the capital of Gujarat?
qs.e: The capital of Gujarat is Gandhinagar. Named after Mahatma Gandhi, it was planned and built by Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru. Gandhinagar has been ranked as the cleanest city in India multiple times in the Swachh Survekshan. The largest city and commercial hub of Gujarat is Ahmedabad. Gujarat was formed on 1 May 1960 after being separated from Maharashtra. The city houses the Gujarat Legislative Assembly and the Raj Bhavan. It is situated on the banks of the Sabarmati River. Gandhinagar is also known for its sectoral planning and green cover.
qs.kf:
☛ What is the capital of Gujarat? → Gandhinagar
☛ Which is the largest city of Gujarat? → Ahmedabad
☛ When was Gujarat formed? → 1 May 1960
☛ On which river is Gandhinagar located? → Sabarmati River
☛ Where is the Gujarat Legislative Assembly located? → Gandhinagar

q: Raja Ravi Verma belongs to the ____________ state.
qs.e: Raja Ravi Verma (1848-1906) was a celebrated Indian painter, considered the pioneer of the Renaissance in Indian art. He was born in Kerala, in the princely state of Travancore, at Kilimanoor. He is famous for his realistic paintings based on Indian epics, especially the Mahabharata and Ramayana. He blended European artistic techniques with Indian themes. His notable works include "Shakuntala" and "Gangavataran". In 2013, the Raja Ravi Varma Award was instituted in his honor by the Kerala government. He is also known for making art accessible through oleographs.
qs.kf:

☛ Who painted "Shakuntala"? → Raja Ravi Verma
☛ What was Raja Ravi Verma's style? → Realistic European style
☛ Who is the pioneer of Renaissance in Indian painting? → Raja Ravi Verma
☛ Which state instituted the Raja Ravi Varma Award? → Kerala

q: What is the full form of FERA?
qs.e: The full form of FERA is Foreign Exchange Regulation Act. It was enacted in India in 1973 to regulate foreign exchange transactions and protect the country's foreign exchange reserves. This act imposed strict controls on the import, export, and exchange of foreign currency. Later, as part of economic reforms, it was replaced by the Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA) in 1999, which was more liberal and simplified. FERA primarily focused on conserving foreign exchange and preventing its misuse, whereas FEMA facilitates foreign exchange management.
qs.kf:
☛ What is the full form of FERA? → Foreign Exchange Regulation Act
☛ When was FERA enacted? → 1973
☛ Which act replaced FERA? → FEMA (Foreign Exchange Management Act)
☛ When was FEMA enacted? → 1999
☛ What was the main objective of FERA? → To regulate foreign exchange transactions

q: Why did the Government of India remove the 'monument of national importance' status from the statue of John Nicholson?
o: The statue was found to be historically inaccurate.
It was considered irrelevant to India's independence struggle.
It was linked to British colonial legacy.
The statue was in a deteriorating condition.
qs.e: John Nicholson was a British army officer who fought brutally against Indians during the 1857 rebellion. Declaring his statue a monument of national importance promoted colonial legacy. The government removed this status to prioritize India's freedom struggle and national pride. This step is part of a policy to remove colonial symbols and promote indigenous heritage. The statue, located in Delhi, was seen as a reminder of British oppression rather than a source of inspiration.
qs.kf:
☛ Location of John Nicholson statue → Delhi
☛ Nicholson's role in 1857 revolt → Fought on British side
☛ Other colonial monuments removed by Indian government → Renamed many roads and buildings

☛ Main objective of removal → Honor heroes of Indian freedom struggle

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (17/06/2025) Shift 1
q: When was the Lokpal and Lokayukta Act came into force in India?
qs.e: The Lokpal and Lokayukta Act, 2013 was passed by the Parliament on 17 December 2013, but it came into force on 16 January 2014. This act establishes the Lokpal, an anti-corruption body in India, which investigates corruption charges against public officials and representatives at the central level. The Lokpal consists of a chairperson and a maximum of eight members, of which half are from judicial background. The act also provides for the establishment of Lokayuktas at the state level. The Lokpal has jurisdiction over all public servants, including the Prime Minister, subject to certain conditions. The act was a result of years of demand for a strong anti-corruption ombudsman.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the Lokpal Act passed? → 17 December 2013
☛ Maximum number of members in Lokpal? → 8 members (9 including chairperson)
☛ Who appoints the Lokpal chairperson? → President of India
☛ Does the Lokpal cover the Prime Minister? → Yes, but with certain conditions
☛ At what level does Lokayukta function? → State level

q: Bill Gates co-founded ‘Microsoft Corporation’ in 1975 with?
qs.e: Bill Gates co-founded Microsoft Corporation in 1975 with Paul G. Allen. The two started the company in Albuquerque, New Mexico, initially developing software for microprocessors. Paul Allen played a crucial role in writing the BASIC interpreter for the MITS Altair 8800, which became Microsoft's first major product. Bill Gates served as CEO and chairman, while Allen provided technical and strategic direction. Their partnership laid the foundation for the personal computer revolution, making Microsoft one of the most influential technology companies globally.
qs.kf:
☛ Who are the co-founders of Microsoft? → Bill Gates and Paul Allen
☛ When was Microsoft founded? → 1975
☛ What was Microsoft's first product? → Altair BASIC
☛ When did Paul Allen pass away? → 2018
☛ What is Bill Gates' current role? → Philanthropist (Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation)

q: Which of these wars took place after India became independent?
qs.e: India became independent on 15 August 1947. World War II (1939-1945) and World War I (1914-1918) occurred before independence. The Boer War (1899-1902) also predates independence. The Gulf War (1990-1991) took place between Iraq and Kuwait; although India did not participate, it happened after India's independence.
qs.kf:
☛ Period of World War I → 1914-1918
☛ Period of World War II → 1939-1945
☛ Period of Boer War → 1899-1902
☛ Date of Indian Independence → 15 August 1947

q: In which year was The Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act introduced in India?
qs.e: The Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act (RTE Act) was passed by the Indian Parliament in the year 2009. It came into effect on 1 April 2010. This act aims to provide free and compulsory education to all children between the ages of 6 and 14 years. It makes education a fundamental right under Article 21A of the Indian Constitution. Prior to this, the 86th Constitutional Amendment in 2002 had inserted Article 21A, but the actual law was enacted in 2009.
qs.kf:
☛ When did RTE Act come into force? → 1 April 2010
☛ Age group covered? → 6-14 years
☛ Under which Article? → Article 21A
☛ Which amendment added Article 21A? → 86th Amendment, 2002
☛ Full name of RTE? → Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009

q: VVPAT is a machine that is used in Indian elections to ensure that the citizen's vote has been correctly placed. What is the full form of VVPAT?
qs.e: The full form of VVPAT is Voter Verifiable Paper Audit Trail. It is a machine attached to an Electronic Voting Machine (EVM). When a voter casts a vote on the EVM, the VVPAT prints a paper slip showing the candidate for whom the vote has been cast. This slip is visible to the voter through a transparent window for about 7 seconds, allowing the voter to verify that their vote has been recorded correctly. After verification, the slip falls into a sealed box. This system was introduced to enhance transparency and credibility in elections. In India, VVPAT was first used in a by-election in Nagaland in 2013.
qs.kf:
☛ Full form of VVPAT → Voter Verifiable Paper Audit Trail
☛ VVPAT is used with which machine → EVM (Electronic Voting Machine)
☛ How long is the VVPAT slip visible → 7 seconds
☛ First use of VVPAT in India → 2013 in Nagaland by-election
☛ Principle of VVPAT → Paper Audit Trail system

q: The Komagata Maru was a_____steamship
qs.e: The Komagata Maru was a Japanese steamship that was chartered in 1914 to carry 376 Indian passengers to Canada. The passengers were mostly Sikh, Muslim, and Hindu immigrants, all British subjects. The Canadian government denied them entry, leading to a violent incident upon their return to Calcutta. This event became a significant turning point in the Indian independence movement, as it fueled resentment against British colonial policies. The ship was owned by Shinsaku Asakura, a Japanese businessman. The incident highlighted issues of racial discrimination and the rights of Indian migrants within the British Empire.
qs.kf:
☛ Which country owned the Komagata Maru? → Japan
☛ In which year did the Komagata Maru incident occur? → 1914
☛ Who was the owner of the ship? → Shinsaku Asakura
☛ How many passengers were on board? → 376
☛ Where did the passengers originate from? → India (mainly Punjab)

q: The concept of 'sustainable development' was introduced by which one of the following reports?
qs.e: The concept of sustainable development was formally introduced by the Brundtland Report (Our Common Future), published in 1987. The report defined sustainable development as development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs. The commission was chaired by Gro Harlem Brundtland, former Prime Minister of Norway. While the Rio Declaration (1992) and Agenda 21 elaborated on the concept, and the Johannesburg Declaration (2002) focused on its implementation, it was the Brundtland Report that first popularized the term globally.
qs.kf:
☛ Year of Brundtland Report publication → 1987
☛ Alternative name of Brundtland Report → Our Common Future
☛ Report that gave definition of sustainable development → Brundtland Report
☛ Chairperson of Brundtland Commission → Gro Harlem Brundtland
☛ Number of principles in Rio Declaration on sustainable development → 27 principles

q: Who has been named as the leader of Opposition in Rajya Sabha in Feb 2021?
qs.e: In February 2021, Mallikarjun Kharge was named the Leader of Opposition in Rajya Sabha. He is a senior leader of the Indian National Congress and a Rajya Sabha member from Karnataka. He succeeded Ghulam Nabi Azad, whose term had ended. Kharge's appointment was seen as a strategic move by the Congress party, as he belongs to the Dalit community and has extensive experience. He has previously served as a Union Minister and was a candidate for the Congress presidency. As Leader of Opposition in Rajya Sabha, his role includes critiquing government policies and coordinating opposition parties.
qs.kf:
☛ Who became Leader of Opposition in Rajya Sabha in Feb 2021? → Mallikarjun Kharge
☛ Who held this position before him? → Ghulam Nabi Azad
☛ Which state does Kharge represent in Rajya Sabha? → Karnataka
☛ Which community does he belong to? → Dalit
☛ Main role of Leader of Opposition in Rajya Sabha? → Criticizing government policies and coordinating opposition

q: Who among the following was the speaker of the Lok Sabha before Om Birla?
qs.e: Om Birla assumed office as the Speaker of the Lok Sabha on 19 June 2019. Before him, Sumitra Mahajan was the Speaker of the 16th Lok Sabha (2014-2019). She was the second woman Speaker of the Lok Sabha (the first being Meira Kumar). Sumitra Mahajan was a member of the Bharatiya Janata Party and served as an eight-time MP from the Indore constituency in Madhya Pradesh. She took oath as Speaker on 6 June 2014. Prior to her, Meira Kumar was the Speaker of the 15th Lok Sabha (2009-2014). Somnath Chatterjee served as Speaker of the 14th Lok Sabha (2004-2009), and Manohar Joshi was Speaker of the 13th Lok Sabha (1999-2004).
qs.kf:
☛ First woman Speaker of Lok Sabha → Meira Kumar (2009-2014)
☛ Second woman Speaker of Lok Sabha → Sumitra Mahajan (2014-2019)
☛ Speaker of 16th Lok Sabha → Sumitra Mahajan
☛ Speaker of 17th Lok Sabha → Om Birla (2019 onwards)
☛ Term of Lok Sabha Speaker → 5 years or until dissolution

q: In which of the following periods was the Second World War fought?
qs.e: The Second World War began on 1 September 1939 with Germany's invasion of Poland and ended on 2 September 1945 with Japan's surrender. It was fought between the Allied Powers (Britain, France, Soviet Union, USA) and the Axis Powers (Germany, Italy, Japan). It was the deadliest conflict in human history, causing around 70 to 80 million casualties. The war led to the formation of the United Nations and the beginning of the Cold War.
qs.kf:
☛ When did World War II start? → 1 September 1939
☛ When did it end? → 2 September 1945
☛ What event started the war? → Germany's invasion of Poland
☛ Which were the Axis Powers? → Germany, Italy, Japan
☛ Which organization was formed after the war? → United Nations

q: Justice M Fathima Beevi was the first female Judge appointed to the Supreme Court of India in 1989. She passed away at the age of 96 on:
qs.e: Justice M Fathima Beevi was the first female judge appointed to the Supreme Court of India in 1989. Born on 30 April 1927 in Kerala, she served as a Supreme Court judge from 1989 to 1992. She later became the Governor of Tamil Nadu. She passed away on 23 November 2023 at the age of 96. Her appointment was a historic step towards diversity in the judiciary. She also served as the first female judge of the Kerala High Court. Justice Beevi's career inspired many women in law. Her legacy continues to be significant in Indian legal history. She was known for her integrity and landmark judgments.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the first female judge of the Supreme Court of India? → Justice M Fathima Beevi
☛ When did Justice M Fathima Beevi serve as a Supreme Court judge? → 1989-1992
☛ After serving as a Supreme Court judge, which position did Fathima Beevi hold? → Governor of Tamil Nadu
☛ Where was Justice M Fathima Beevi born? → Kerala
☛ Which High Court had Fathima Beevi as its first female judge? → Kerala High Court

q: Which colonial power held Yanaon (Yanam) and Chandernagore as part of its possessions in India?
qs.e: Yanaon (Yanam) and Chandernagore were part of the French colonial possessions in India. France established trading centers in India during the 17th century and gradually gained control over Pondicherry, Karaikal, Mahe, Yanaon, and Chandernagore. These territories were under the French East India Company and later administered by the French government. In 1954, these territories were integrated into India. Chandernagore is located in West Bengal, while Yanaon is part of the Union Territory of Puducherry. Thus, both these places were under French colonial power.
qs.kf:
☛ Capital of French India → Pondicherry
☛ First French factory in India → Surat (1668)
☛ Major conflict between French and British → Carnatic Wars
☛ French governor who developed Pondicherry → François Martin
☛ Year of merger of French India → 1954

q: Which of the following was built by the ancient Incas?
qs.e: Machu Picchu was built by the ancient Incas in the 15th century. It is a famous citadel located in the Andes Mountains of Peru and is often called the 'Lost City of the Incas.' It was rediscovered by American explorer Hiram Bingham in 1911. Other options: City of Petra (built by Nabataeans in Jordan), Hagia Sophia (built by Byzantine Emperor Justinian in Istanbul, Turkey), and Acropolis (built by ancient Greeks in Athens, Greece) are not related to the Inca civilization. Machu Picchu was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1983.
qs.kf:
☛ In which country is Machu Picchu located? → Peru
☛ Which civilization built Machu Picchu? → Inca civilization
☛ In which mountain range is Machu Picchu situated? → Andes Mountains
☛ Who rediscovered Machu Picchu? → Hiram Bingham (1911)
☛ In which year was Machu Picchu declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site? → 1983

q: Which of the following years was not happened the Indo-Pak war?
qs.e: The major wars between India and Pakistan occurred in 1947, 1965, 1971, and 1999. In the year 1962, there was no Indo-Pak war; instead, India fought a war with China due to a border dispute. The first war in 1947 was over Kashmir, resulting in the creation of the Line of Control. The 1971 war led to the formation of Bangladesh. In 1999, the Kargil War took place, involving Pakistani infiltrators and the Indian Army. Thus, only the year 1962 is not associated with an Indo-Pak war.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the first Indo-Pak war? → 1947
☛ In which year did the India-China war occur? → 1962
☛ Which country was formed after the 1971 war? → Bangladesh
☛ When did the Kargil War take place? → 1999
☛ What was the main issue in the 1965 Indo-Pak war? → Kashmir

q: The Gateway of India in Mumbai was built to welcome:
qs.e: The Gateway of India is a historic monument located in Mumbai, built in 1911 to welcome the British monarch King George V and his wife Queen Mary on their visit to India. Designed by architect George Wittet, the monument was completed and opened in 1924. It is built in the Indo-Saracenic style and is one of Mumbai's major tourist attractions. The Gateway of India also served as a symbolic entrance to India during the British Raj.
qs.kf:
☛ Where is the Gateway of India located? → Mumbai
☛ When was the construction of Gateway of India started? → 1911
☛ Who designed the Gateway of India? → George Wittet

☛ When was the Gateway of India inaugurated? → 1924

q: What is the budgetary disinvestment target of the Union government of India for FY20?
qs.e: For the financial year 2019-20, the Union government set a disinvestment target of ₹1,05,000 crore, which was significantly higher than previous years. This target was announced by Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman in the FY20 Budget. To achieve this, the government planned to sell its stake in various public sector undertakings, including a major initial public offering (IPO) of Life Insurance Corporation (LIC). However, due to the COVID-19 pandemic, the government could not meet the target, and actual disinvestment remained lower. Disinvestment is a crucial part of government revenue, used to reduce fiscal deficit and fund infrastructure projects. The target reflects the government's commitment to privatize and raise capital.
qs.kf:
☛ What was the disinvestment target for FY20? → ₹1,05,000 crore
☛ Who presented the FY20 Budget? → Nirmala Sitharaman
☛ What is the purpose of disinvestment? → Raise revenue and reduce fiscal deficit
☛ Was the FY20 disinvestment target met? → No, due to COVID-19
☛ Which major disinvestment was planned? → LIC IPO (later deferred)

q: What was 26th January called in India before 1947?
qs.e: Before 1947, 26th January was celebrated as Independence Day in India. In 1929, the Lahore Session of the Indian National Congress passed the Purna Swaraj resolution, and on 26th January 1930, the first Independence Day was observed. This tradition continued annually until 1947. After India gained independence in 1947, the Constitution was adopted on 26th November 1949 and came into effect on 26th January 1950, which was then declared as Republic Day. Independence Day is now celebrated on 15th August. Thus, before 1947, 26th January was called Independence Day.
qs.kf:
☛ In which Congress session was Purna Swaraj resolution passed? → Lahore Session
☛ Which day was first celebrated on 26th January 1930? → Independence Day
☛ When is Republic Day celebrated in India? → 26th January
☛ When did the Constitution of India come into effect? → 26th January 1950
☛ Who moved the Purna Swaraj resolution? → Jawaharlal Nehru

q: Which Indian state was in ancient history known as Kamarupa?
qs.e: In ancient India, Kamarupa was a prominent kingdom located in the present-day region of Assam. It was a powerful empire in eastern India with its capital at Pragjyotishpur (modern Guwahati). Kamarupa is mentioned in several ancient texts like the Mahabharata, Ramayana, and Puranas. The kingdom existed during the Gupta period and beyond, extending over parts of present-day Assam, Bangladesh, Bhutan, and Myanmar. The Kamarupa dynasty ruled from the 7th to 12th century CE, with notable rulers like Bhaskaravarman.

☛ In which texts is Kamarupa mentioned? → Mahabharata, Ramayana, Puranas
☛ Who was a famous ruler of the Kamarupa dynasty? → Bhaskaravarman
☛ In which modern state is Kamarupa located? → Assam
☛ Which regions did Kamarupa extend to? → Present-day Assam, Bangladesh, Bhutan, Myanmar

q: When did Lord Clive finally return to England from India?
qs.e: Lord Clive left India in 1765 but stopped at Madras and finally reached England in 1767. His final departure from India occurred in 1767. Although he began his journey from Bengal in 1765, a stopover at Madras delayed his arrival in England until 1767. Lord Clive, as Governor of Bengal, strengthened the British East India Company's position after the Battle of Plassey (1757). He served two terms in India: first from 1744 to 1753 and second from 1755 to 1767. Thus, his definitive return to England was in 1767.
qs.kf:
☛ Battle of Plassey year → 1757
☛ Lord Clive's first Indian tenure → 1744-1753
☛ Lord Clive's second Indian tenure → 1755-1767
☛ Nawab defeated by Clive → Siraj-ud-Daulah
☛ Lord Clive's birth year → 1725

q: Under which writ the court orders a lower court or another authority to transfer a matter pending before it to the higher authority or court?
qs.e: Certiorari is a writ issued by a higher court (such as a High Court or the Supreme Court) to a lower court or quasi-judicial body, ordering it to transfer a pending matter to the higher court. This writ is typically used when the lower court has exceeded its jurisdiction or violated principles of natural justice. It can also be issued to quash the decision of the lower court or send the case back for reconsideration. In India, Certiorari is issued under Article 32 and Article 226 of the Constitution. It serves as an important tool for judicial review, ensuring that lower authorities act within their legal limits and adhere to fair procedures.
qs.kf:
☛ Purpose of Certiorari → To transfer a case from a lower court to a higher court when the lower court acts beyond its jurisdiction
☛ When Certiorari is issued → When the lower court violates principles of natural justice
☛ Which court issues Certiorari → High Court or Supreme Court
☛ Meaning of Certiorari → To be certified or to be verified
☛ Types of writs in Indian Constitution → Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, Quo Warranto

q: In which of the following years was the Sino-Indian War (Indo-China War) fought?
qs.e: The Sino-Indian War was fought in the year 1962. This war occurred between India and China due to border disputes, primarily in the regions of Arunachal Pradesh (then North-East Frontier Agency) and Aksai Chin. China launched a surprise attack in October 1962. The war lasted for about a month, and China unilaterally declared a ceasefire. The Indian Army suffered heavy losses, which led India to make significant changes in its defense policy. This event continues to impact the relations between the two countries today.

☛ Year of Sino-Indian War → 1962
☛ Prime Minister of India during the war → Jawaharlal Nehru
☛ President of China during the war → Mao Zedong
☛ Main cause of the war → Border dispute (McMahon Line and Aksai Chin)
☛ Outcome of the war → China's unilateral ceasefire and withdrawal

q: In which year was India declared a Republic?
qs.e: India was declared a Republic on January 26, 1950. On this day, the Constitution of India came into effect, making the country a sovereign, socialist, secular, and democratic republic. The date January 26 was chosen because on this day in 1930, the Indian National Congress had declared Purna Swaraj (complete independence). Dr. Rajendra Prasad became the first President of India. Becoming a republic marked India's complete freedom from British rule and its establishment as a republic with its own constitution.

☛ What is the capital of India? → New Delhi

q: In which year was the Aam Aadmi Party founded?
qs.e: The Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) was founded in the year 2012. It was established by Arvind Kejriwal and his associates, who emerged from the India Against Corruption movement. The party was formally founded on 26 November 2012 with the goal of fighting corruption and addressing issues of the common man. AAP achieved significant success in its first electoral contest, the Delhi Legislative Assembly election in 2013, and formed the government. The party's symbol is a broom, representing cleanliness and the fight against corruption.

q: Which of the following eminent persons called the Indian Constitution as 'Lawyer’s Paradise and difficult to understand by common Citizen'?
qs.e: The eminent person who called the Indian Constitution a 'Lawyer's Paradise and difficult to understand by common citizen' is Ivor Jenning. He was a British constitutional expert who criticized the Indian Constitution for its excessive legal language and detailed provisions, making it hard for ordinary citizens to comprehend. In contrast, Granville Austin described it as a 'document of social revolution', while K.C. Wheare called it a mixture of federal and unitary features. Morris Jones worked on the implementation of the constitution. Ivor Jenning's remark highlights the complexity and verbosity of the Indian Constitution, which contains many legal intricacies that require expert interpretation.
qs.kf:
☛ Who called the Indian Constitution a 'Lawyer's Paradise'? → Ivor Jenning
☛ Who described the Indian Constitution as a 'document of social revolution'? → Granville Austin
☛ Who said the Indian Constitution is a mixture of federal and unitary? → K.C. Wheare
☛ Which British constitutional expert commented on the Indian Constitution? → Ivor Jenning
☛ What did Ivor Jenning say about the Indian Constitution? → Lawyer's Paradise and difficult for common citizens

q: The Ramosi Revolt was led by which tribal leader in 1822 against Britishers?
qs.e: The Ramosi Revolt took place in 1822 against the British in the Satara region of Maharashtra. It was led by the tribal leader Chittur Singh. The Ramosi tribe primarily inhabited the Western Ghats and Deccan plateau areas. This revolt was a result of tribal discontent and heavy taxation under British rule. Chittur Singh united the local Ramosi community and launched an armed struggle against the British. However, the British army crushed the revolt and captured Chittur Singh. This uprising is an important part of India's tribal resistance movements.
qs.kf:
☛ Leader of Ramosi Revolt → Chittur Singh
☛ Year → 1822
☛ Region → Satara, Maharashtra
☛ Tribe → Ramosi
☛ Cause of revolt → British rule and heavy taxation

q: In September 2025, the Supreme Court of India reaffirmed which important legal position under the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989?
o: The grant of anticipatory bail is absolutely barred if the FIR prima facie discloses an offence under the Act
The accused can apply for anticipatory bail under all circumstances
The anticipatory bail provision has been removed from the Indian Penal Code
The anticipatory bail may be granted only by the High Court
qs.e: In September 2025, the Supreme Court of India upheld the constitutional validity of Sections 18 and 18A of the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989. These sections provide that if the FIR prima facie discloses an offence under the Act, the grant of anticipatory bail is absolutely barred. The Court held that this restriction protects the objectives of the Act and safeguards SC/ST communities from harassment. This decision came in the case of Sunil Kumar Upadhyay vs State of Uttar Pradesh (2025).
qs.kf:
☛ Which sections of the SC/ST Act impose a bar on anticipatory bail? → Sections 18 and 18A
☛ In which case did the Supreme Court uphold the bar on anticipatory bail? → Sunil Kumar Upadhyay vs State of Uttar Pradesh (2025)
☛ When was the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act enacted? → 1989
☛ When can anticipatory bail be granted under this Act? → Only if the FIR does not prima facie disclose an offence
☛ What is the purpose of this restriction? → To protect SC/ST communities from harassment

q: The Indian government unveiled which of the following guidelines in November 2025, which are comprehensive frameworks to ensure safe, inclusive and responsible AI adoption across various sectors and propose a robust governance framework to foster cutting-edge innovation and safely develop and deploy AI?
qs.e: The Indian government unveiled the India AI Governance Guidelines in November 2025, which are comprehensive frameworks to ensure safe, inclusive, and responsible AI adoption across various sectors. ☛ What is their benefit? → Foster innovation and safe AI development

q: What is the name of the Act passed by the Indian Parliament in August 2025 to regulate online gaming and restrict online money games?
o: Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Act, 2025
qs.e: This Act was passed by the Indian Parliament in August 2025 to regulate online gaming and restrict online money games. It empowers the central government to create a national framework in coordination with states. The Act establishes a National Online Gaming Authority as the apex regulatory body. It distinguishes between skill-based and chance-based games. The Act aims to protect minors and prevent financial fraud. It also mandates that online gaming platforms must register with the authority to operate legally.

q: What is the mass of the moon?
qs.e: The mass of the Moon is approximately 7.347 × 1022 kg, which is about 1.2% of Earth's mass. The Moon's density is 3.34 g/cm3, lower than Earth's. Gravitational acceleration on the Moon is about 1/6 that of Earth. The Moon's mass plays a key role in the Earth-Moon system, affecting tides. Its radius is about 1737 km.

q: 'Kimono' is the traditional dress of-
qs.e: Kimono is the traditional dress of Japan, which has been a symbol of Japanese culture for centuries. It is a long, robe-like garment tied with a sash called an obi. Kimono is traditionally made of silk and features intricate designs and colors. It is worn on special occasions such as weddings, festivals, and tea ceremonies. Both men and women wear kimonos, though their styles and colors differ. Other options: China's traditional dress is the cheongsam or changshan, New Zealand's Maori wear traditional clothing, and Korea wears hanbok.

q: Which of the following Japanese terms in 5S methodology represents the meaning of shine?
qs.e: The 5S methodology is a Japanese management technique used to organize and maintain a clean and efficient workplace. Its five steps are: Seiri (Sort), Seiton (Set in order), Seiso (Shine), Seiketsu (Standardize), and Shitsuke (Sustain). The term 'Seiso' means keeping the work area clean, removing dust and debris, and ensuring that all equipment is in good working condition. This step contributes to safety, quality, and productivity. Among the options: Seiri stands for sorting, Shitsuke for discipline, and Seiton for arranging. Therefore, Seiso is the correct term for 'shine'.

☛ Japanese term for 'set in order' in 5S → Seiton

☛ Fifth step of 5S → Shitsuke

q: Which of these religions do the Jews follow?
qs.e: Jews follow Judaism, a monotheistic religion. It is one of the oldest religions in the world, originating approximately 4000 years ago in the Middle East. Followers of Judaism believe in one omnipotent God, often referred to as Yahweh. Its primary sacred text is the Torah (the Hebrew Bible), which contains 613 commandments. Important Jewish festivals include Yom Kippur (Day of Atonement), Hanukkah (Festival of Lights), and Passover (Pesach). Judaism has influenced the development of both Christianity and Islam. There are about 14 million Jews worldwide today. The religion is deeply rooted in tradition, law, and community.

☛ Founder of Judaism → Considered to be Abraham
☛ Primary religious text → Torah
☛ Place of worship → Synagogue
☛ Name of God → Yahweh or Elohim
☛ Major symbol → Star of David

q: Which of these states was NOT divided in the year 2000?
qs.e: In the year 2000, three Indian states were reorganized. Madhya Pradesh was divided to form Chhattisgarh, Uttar Pradesh was divided to form Uttarakhand (then Uttaranchal), and Bihar was divided to form Jharkhand. These three new states came into existence on 1 November 2000. Maharashtra was not divided in this year. Maharashtra was formed on 1 May 1960 on linguistic grounds. Thus, only Maharashtra remained undivided.

q: When was Leprosy Day celebrated?
qs.e: Anti-Leprosy Day is observed annually on 30 January, the death anniversary of Mahatma Gandhi. The day aims to raise awareness about leprosy and eliminate associated stigma. Mahatma Gandhi showed compassion towards leprosy patients and worked for their upliftment. In India, this day holds special significance as it pays tribute to the Father of the Nation and reflects commitment to leprosy eradication. According to the World Health Organization, World Leprosy Day is observed on the last Sunday of January, but India observes it on 30 January.

☛ Causative bacterium of leprosy → Mycobacterium leprae

☛ Treatment for leprosy → Multi Drug Therapy (MDT)

q: Which of the following is a vertical restructuring method?
A. Job rotation
B. Job growth
C. Job promotion
D. Job evaluation
qs.e: Vertical restructuring involves increasing an employee's responsibility, authority, and position, which is seen in job promotion. Job promotion moves an employee to a higher level, enabling them to handle more complex tasks. In contrast, job rotation is a horizontal movement where employees work at the same level across different departments. Job growth relates to skill development, not structural change. Job evaluation is a process of assessing job worth. Thus, the correct example of vertical restructuring is job promotion.
qs.kf:

q: A new dimension added by Amartya Sen to food security is:
qs.e: Amartya Sen introduced a new dimension to the concept of food security, known as entitlements. He argued that food security is not just about the availability of food or its affordability, but also about an individual's ability to command that food. In his influential work 'Poverty and Famines', Sen demonstrated that famines occur not because of food shortage but due to the failure of entitlement— people lose the legal, social, or economic means to obtain food. Therefore, food security must include the aspect of entitlement, which refers to the set of commodity bundles that a person can legitimately acquire using their resources and rights. This dimension shifts the focus from food supply to people's capacity to access food.
qs.kf:
☛ New dimension added by Amartya Sen to food security → Entitlements
☛ Main cause of famines according to Sen → Lack of access to food, not food shortage
☛ Famous book by Amartya Sen → Poverty and Famines
☛ Meaning of entitlement → Legal or social right to obtain a commodity
☛ Traditional dimensions of food security → Availability, affordability, sustainable livelihoods

q: In which simple multi-cellular organism does sporangia develop on hyphae and spore formation occurs in sporangia?
qs.e: The question describes a simple multicellular organism where sporangia develop on hyphae and spore formation occurs within these sporangia. These spores are dispersed to germinate into new fungal colonies. Leishmania is a protozoan parasite causing kala-azar, not multicellular. Yeast is a unicellular fungus that reproduces by budding. q: Which of the following are cultivated for the pearls they make?
qs.e: Pearl cultivation involves oysters, which are marine bivalve mollusks belonging to the family Ostreidae. Pearls form when an irritant (like a sand grain) enters the oyster's shell. The oyster secretes layers of nacre (mother-of-pearl) around the irritant, creating a pearl over time. This process is called biomineralization. Oysters are specifically cultivated in pearl farms through pearl aquaculture, where irritants are intentionally inserted to stimulate pearl production. Option 1 (Sardines), Option 2 (Prawns), and Option 3 (Pomfrets) are incorrect because they are fish or crustaceans used primarily as food sources, not for pearl production. Sardines are small oily fish (Clupeidae family), prawns are decapod crustaceans, and pomfrets are marine fish (Stromateidae family). None possess the nacre-secreting mantle tissue required for pearl formation.

q: The members of phylum ________ are exclusively free-living marine animals.
qs.e: The question asks about a phylum whose members are exclusively free-living marine animals. In the Animal Kingdom, Echinodermata is the only phylum where all members are marine and free-living. Examples include starfish (Asterias rubens), sea urchins, and sea cucumbers. They are characterized by a spiny skin, water vascular system for locomotion, and radial symmetry in adults (bilateral in larvae). Why Option 4 is correct: Echinoderms are entirely marine and free-living; no parasitic or freshwater forms exist. Why other options are incorrect: - Mollusca (Option 1): Includes marine (e.g., octopus), freshwater (e.g., snails), and terrestrial (e.g., slugs) species; not exclusively marine. - Nematoda (Option 2): Includes free-living (soil, marine) and parasitic forms (e.g., Ascaris lumbricoides); not exclusively marine. - Arthropoda (Option 3): Includes marine (e.g., crabs), freshwater, terrestrial, and aerial species; highly diverse habitats.

q: Which of the following animals shows the power of regeneration?
qs.e: Regeneration is the biological process where an organism can regrow lost or damaged body parts. Among the given options, Planaria (a type of flatworm) exhibits remarkable regenerative abilities due to the presence of neoblasts (pluripotent stem cells) distributed throughout its body. When cut into pieces, each fragment can regenerate into a complete organism through cell proliferation and differentiation. In contrast, Earthworms show limited regeneration, typically only regrowing anterior segments under specific conditions. Ticks (arachnids) and Leeches (annelids) lack significant regenerative capabilities; they cannot regenerate entire body parts like Planaria can. This makes Planaria a classic model organism in regeneration studies.

☛ Their regeneration is driven by neoblasts, which are totipotent stem cells making up about 25–30% of their cells.
☛ Other animals with high regenerative ability include Hydra (Cnidaria) and starfish (Echinodermata).
☛ In humans, limited regeneration occurs in tissues like the liver and epidermis. Important One-liners for Upcoming Exams:

q: Select a term to complete the given analogy. Binary Fission : Bacteria :: Fragmentation : _________
qs.e: The analogy relates asexual reproduction methods to the organisms that commonly exhibit them. Binary fission is a type of asexual reproduction where a single parent cell divides into two equal daughter cells; it is characteristic of prokaryotes like bacteria (e.g., Escherichia coli). Similarly, fragmentation is an asexual reproduction method where the parent body breaks into fragments, each growing into a new individual; it is commonly observed in multicellular organisms with simple body organization, such as algae (e.g., Spirogyra). Option 2 (Algae) is correct because algae like Spirogyrareproduce asexually by fragmentation. Option 1 (Birds), Option 3 (Mammals), and Option 4 (Insects) are incorrect as these are complex animals that reproduce sexually, not by fragmentation.

q: In which of the following organisms are chromoplasts present?
qs.e: Chromoplasts are specialized plastids containing pigments (carotenoids, xanthophylls) that give color to flowers, fruits, and some roots. They are found exclusively in plant cells and some algae, not in animal cells. Rose (a flowering plant) contains chromoplasts in its petals, which provide red, yellow, or orange coloration. Amoeba (a protozoan) lacks plastids entirely as it is a unicellular animal-like organism. Hydra (a freshwater cnidarian) and starfish (an echinoderm) are both animals and do not possess chromoplasts; animal cells lack plastids altogether. Chromoplasts develop from chloroplasts or other plastids and help in pollination by attracting pollinators.
qs.kf:
☛ Chromoplasts contain carotenoid pigments (carotene, xanthophylls) but lack chlorophyll.
☛ They are non-photosynthetic plastids found in fruits (tomato, mango), flowers (marigold, rose), and roots (carrot).
☛ Chromoplasts develop from chloroplasts during fruit ripening (e.g., green tomato → red tomato).
☛ Leucoplasts are colorless plastids that store starch, oils, or proteins.
☛ Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll and are responsible for photosynthesis in plants. Important One-liners for Upcoming Exams:
☛ Which plastids give color to flowers and fruits? → Chromoplasts
☛ Chromoplasts contain which pigments? → Carotenoids (carotene, xanthophylls)
☛ Which cell organelle is absent in animal cells? → Plastids (chloroplasts, chromoplasts, leucoplasts)
☛ Tomato fruit turns red due to which plastid? → Chromoplasts
☛ Colorless plastids that store starch are called? → Leucoplasts

q: Through the phenomenon of biological magnification, which of the following has the maximum concentration of pesticides in them?
qs.e: Biological magnification (or biomagnification) is the process where certain substances like pesticides (e.g., DDT) or heavy metals increase in concentration at successive trophic levels in a food chain. This occurs because these substances are non-biodegradable and lipid-soluble, accumulating in organisms' tissues rather than being excreted. In a typical terrestrial food chain: Grass (producer) → Grasshopper (primary consumer) → Frog (secondary consumer) → Snake (tertiary consumer). Pesticides sprayed on grass are absorbed in small amounts. Grasshoppers eating contaminated grass accumulate more pesticides. Frogs eating multiple grasshoppers further concentrate pesticides. Snakes, as top predators eating many frogs, accumulate the maximum concentration due to cumulative intake over their lifespan. Thus, Snake has the highest pesticide concentration. Grass has the lowest as the entry point. Grasshopper and Frog have intermediate concentrations.
qs.kf:
☛ Biological magnification primarily affects top carnivores like eagles, hawks, and large fish.
☛ Common biomagnifying substances include DDT, mercury, and PCBs (polychlorinated biphenyls).
☛ These substances cause egg-shell thinning in birds, leading to population decline.
☛ Biomagnification occurs in both aquatic and terrestrial food chains.
☛ The bioconcentration factor measures accumulation from environment to organism. Important One-liners for Upcoming Exams:
☛ What is biological magnification? → Increase in concentration of non-biodegradable substances at higher trophic levels.
☛ Which trophic level has maximum DDT concentration? → Top carnivores/tertiary consumers.
☛ Why does DDT accumulate in organisms? → It is lipid-soluble and non-biodegradable.
☛ What is the main effect of DDT on birds? → Egg-shell thinning leading to reproductive failure.
☛ Give an example of biomagnification in aquatic ecosystem? → Mercury accumulation in large fish like tuna.

q: Which single-celled organism divides into many daughter cells simultaneously by multiple fission?
qs.e: Multiple fission is a type of asexual reproduction where a single parent cell divides simultaneously into many daughter cells. Plasmodium (the malaria parasite) exhibits this process during its life cycle in the human liver. In multiple fission, the nucleus divides repeatedly without cytoplasmic division, forming a multinucleated cell called a schizont, which then splits into numerous merozoites. Plasmodium is correct because it undergoes schizogony (a form of multiple fission) in liver cells. Amoeba reproduces by binary fission (dividing into two). Yeast reproduces by budding (forming a small outgrowth). Leishmania reproduces by binary fission in the human host.
qs.kf:
☛ Plasmodium is transmitted by female Anopheles mosquitoes.
☛ Malaria symptoms include cyclic fever, chills, and anemia due to RBC destruction.
☛ Multiple fission also occurs in some algae (e.g., Chlamydomonas) under unfavorable conditions.
☛ Amoeba uses pseudopodia for movement and feeding, not reproduction.
☛ Leishmania causes kala-azar (visceral leishmaniasis) and shows a flagellum in promastigote stage. Important One-liners for Upcoming Exams:
☛ Which parasite causes malaria? → Plasmodium(transmitted by Anopheles mosquito)
☛ What is multiple fission? → Simultaneous division into many daughter cells
☛ How does Amoeba reproduce? → Binary fission (divides into two)
☛ Which process does Plasmodium use in liver cells? → Schizogony (multiple fission)
☛ What is the vector for malaria? → Female Anopheles mosquito

q: Which of the following causes kala-azar?
qs.e: Kala-azar (also known as visceral leishmaniasis) is caused by a protozoan parasite of the genus Leishmania. The specific causative organism is Leishmania donovani. This disease is transmitted through the bite of infected female sandflies (genus Phlebotomus in Old World, Lutzomyia in New World). The parasite infects the reticuloendothelial system, particularly affecting the spleen, liver, and bone marrow. Symptoms include prolonged fever, weight loss, anemia, and enlargement of the spleen and liver. Option 4 (Protozoa) is correct because Leishmania is a protozoan. Option 1 (Fungi) is incorrect as fungi cause diseases like ringworm, not kala-azar. Option 2 (Virus) is incorrect as viruses cause diseases like dengue or influenza. Option 3 (Bacteria) is incorrect as bacteria cause diseases like tuberculosis or cholera.
qs.kf:
☛ Kala-azar is also called Dum-dum fever and black fever.
☛ The disease is endemic in parts of India, Bangladesh, Nepal, Sudan, and Brazil.
☛ Diagnosis is confirmed by detecting amastigotes (Leishman-Donovan bodies) in tissue aspirates.
☛ Treatment includes drugs like sodium stibogluconate and miltefosine.
☛ Post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis (PKDL) can occur as a complication after treatment. Important One-liners for Upcoming Exams:
☛ Which parasite causes kala-azar? → Leishmania donovani

☛ Kala-azar is also known as? → Visceral leishmaniasis or Dum-dum fever
☛ Kala-azar is endemic in which Indian state? → Bihar (and parts of Jharkhand, West Bengal, Uttar Pradesh)

q: Which of the following organisms does NOT show asexual reproduction by means of fission?
qs.e: The question asks which organism does NOT reproduce asexually through fission. Fission is an asexual reproduction method where a parent organism splits into two or more daughter organisms. Leishmania (causative agent of kala-azar) reproduces by binary fission in its promastigote form. Amoeba (Amoeba proteus) reproduces asexually through binary fission, dividing into two daughter cells. Plasmodium (malaria parasite) undergoes multiple fission (schizogony) in human liver and red blood cells. Earthworms (Pheretima posthuma) are hermaphroditic animals that reproduce sexually through cross-fertilization, not by fission. They exchange sperm during copulation and lay eggs in cocoons.

q: Which of these animals has a coat of spines to protect itself?
qs.e: The question asks which animal has a coat of spines for protection. This refers to a specific defensive adaptation in the animal kingdom. The hedgehog (family Erinaceidae) possesses a distinctive covering of stiff, sharp spines (modified hairs made of keratin) that serve as its primary defense mechanism. When threatened, hedgehogs curl into a tight ball, exposing only their spines to deter predators. In contrast, the giant panda has thick fur but no spines; the antelope relies on speed and horns; and the reindeer has antlers and fur, not spines. Thus, only the hedgehog exhibits this specific morphological adaptation.

q: A poultry farmer wants birds that consume less feed, tolerate high heat, and produce quality chicks. Which strategy should he follow?
qs.e: The poultry farmer should follow cross-breeding between exotic and local poultry breeds. This strategy combines desirable traits from both parent types. Exotic breeds (like Leghorn) are selected for high egg production and quality chicks, while indigenous breeds (like Aseel) exhibit better heat tolerance and lower feed requirements due to adaptation to local conditions. q: Which of these insects have teeth?
qs.e: Insects possess specialized mouthparts adapted to their feeding habits, not true teeth like vertebrates. Wasps and beetles have mandibulate mouthparts with strong, toothed mandibles used for biting, chewing, and cutting solid food. Wasps use them to capture prey and manipulate materials, while beetles employ them for feeding on plants, fungi, or other insects. In contrast, butterflies have siphoning mouthparts (proboscis) for liquid feeding, flies have sponging mouthparts for soaking liquids, and bees have chewing-lapping mouthparts with mandibles for handling wax/pollen but primarily lap nectar. Thus, only wasps and beetles exhibit prominent toothed structures functionally analogous to teeth.

☛ Mosquitoes have piercing-sucking mouthparts for blood-feeding, with stylets that penetrate skin.

q: Which of the following organisms shows the phenomenon of regeneration?
qs.e: Regeneration is the biological process where an organism can regrow lost or damaged body parts. Among the given options, Planaria (a type of flatworm) is well-known for its remarkable regenerative abilities. When cut into pieces, each fragment can regenerate into a complete new individual due to the presence of neoblasts (totipotent stem cells) distributed throughout its body. In contrast, Mosquito (insect), House fly (insect), and Honey bee (insect) belong to the phylum Arthropoda and class Insecta, which generally have limited regenerative capacity —they can only regenerate certain tissues during larval stages but cannot regenerate entire organisms from body fragments like Planaria can.

q: Who/What are the natural hosts of Nipah virus?
qs.e: The Nipah virus is a zoonotic pathogen that causes severe respiratory illness and encephalitis in humans. Its natural reservoir hosts are fruit bats (family Pteropodidae), particularly species like Pteropus giganteus(Indian flying fox). These bats carry the virus without showing symptoms, shedding it through saliva, urine, and feces. Option 4 (Fruit bats) is correct because they are the primary wildlife reservoir where the virus circulates naturally. Option 1 (Birds) is incorrect as birds are not known reservoirs for Nipah virus. Option 2 (Pigs) and Option 3 (Goats) are incorrect because while pigs can be intermediate hosts (amplifying the virus during outbreaks), and goats may occasionally get infected, they are not the natural hosts where the virus persists in nature.

q: An organism feeding on multiple hosts in its lifetime is called-
qs.e: In ecology, organisms are classified based on their feeding relationships. A predator is an organism that hunts, kills, and consumes multiple prey organisms (hosts) throughout its lifetime for nutrition. This differs from a parasite (option 2), which lives on or in a single host organism, deriving nutrients without immediately killing it. A parasitoid (option 1) is a specialized organism (often insects like wasps) whose larvae feed on and eventually kill a single host. A saprophyte (option 3) feeds on dead and decaying organic matter, not living hosts. Predators like lions, hawks, or spiders actively hunt multiple prey individuals during their life cycle, making option 4 correct.

q: In which phylum are the animals warm blooded?
qs.e: The question asks about the phylum containing warm-blooded animals. Warm-blooded (endothermic) animals maintain a constant internal body temperature regardless of the environment. Among the given options, only Aves (birds) are warm-blooded. Pisces (fish) are cold-blooded (ectothermic) aquatic vertebrates with gills. Amphibians (like frogs) are cold-blooded vertebrates that live both in water and on land. Reptiles (like snakes) are cold-blooded terrestrial vertebrates with dry scaly skin. Birds possess feathers, beaks, and lay hard-shelled eggs, and their endothermy allows sustained flight and activity in various climates.

q: Which of the following living organisms have bones that help in body movements?
qs.e: The question asks which organism has bones that aid in body movement. Snakes are vertebrates belonging to the class Reptilia and possess an endoskeleton made of bones, including a vertebral column (backbone) and ribs, which provide structural support and enable movement through muscular contractions. In contrast, cockroaches (class Insecta) have an exoskeleton made of chitin, not bones. Earthworms (phylum Annelida) are invertebrates with a hydrostatic skeleton (fluid-filled body cavity) and no bones. Snails (phylum Mollusca) are invertebrates with a calcareous shell but no internal bones. Thus, only snakes have true bones that facilitate movement.

q: The member of which group is usually called a sponge?
qs.e: Sponges belong to the phylum Porifera, which are the simplest multicellular animals. They are characterized by a porous body with numerous pores (ostia) and canals for water circulation, and they lack true tissues and organs. The name "Porifera" means "pore-bearing," referring to their unique body structure. Sponges are aquatic, mostly marine, and have a cellular level of organization. They are filter feeders, using specialized cells called choanocytes (collar cells) to trap food particles from water. Option 3 is correct because Porifera is the scientific phylum for sponges. Option 1 (Tinophora) is incorrect; it might refer to Ctenophora(comb jellies), which are different. Option 2 (Sylentreta) is incorrect; it seems misspelled and not a valid phylum. Option 4 (Platyhelmanties) is incorrect; it likely refers to Platyhelminthes(flatworms), which are more complex.

q: Hormones are normally absent in-
qs.e: Hormones are chemical messengers produced by multicellular organisms, primarily in endocrine glands, to regulate physiological processes. They are absent in bacteria because bacteria are unicellular prokaryotes lacking specialized endocrine systems. In contrast, rats, monkeys, and cats are multicellular animals with well-developed endocrine systems that produce hormones like insulin, adrenaline, and thyroxine. Bacteria use simpler signaling molecules like autoinducers for quorum sensing, but these are not classified as true hormones. Hormones typically require complex receptor mechanisms found in eukaryotic cells, which bacteria lack.

q: Which of the following is/are NOT a parasitic organism?
qs.e: Amoeba is a free-living, unicellular protozoan that obtains nutrition through holozoic mode (phagocytosis) and is not parasitic. In contrast, Ticks (arachnids) and Lice (insects) are ectoparasites that feed on host blood. Cuscuta (dodder plant) is a parasitic angiosperm that lacks chlorophyll and derives nutrients from host plants via haustoria. Parasitism involves a host-parasite relationship where the parasite benefits at the host's expense. Amoeba's free-living nature and independent feeding distinguish it from true parasites. q: Which creature grows again after it is cut into half?
qs.e: The correct answer is Earthworm because it exhibits remarkable regeneration capability. When cut into two halves, the anterior (head) portion containing the cerebral ganglia and vital organs can regenerate a new posterior end, while the posterior portion may also regenerate a new anterior end under favorable conditions. This occurs due to the presence of pluripotent stem cells called neoblasts in their segmented body. In contrast, Cockroaches (arthropods) have limited regeneration ability only for appendages, not body halves. Lizards can regenerate tails through autotomy, but not entire body halves. Frogs (amphibians) show limited regeneration only during tadpole stage, not as adults.

q: Sleeping sickness is caused by:
qs.e: Sleeping sickness, also known as African trypanosomiasis, is caused by the protozoan parasite Trypanosoma brucei. This disease is transmitted to humans through the bite of an infected tsetse fly (genus Glossina). The tsetse fly acts as a biological vector, injecting the parasite into the bloodstream during its blood meal. The parasite then multiplies in the blood and lymphatic system, eventually invading the central nervous system, leading to neurological symptoms including sleep disturbances, confusion, and coma if untreated. Option 1 (Mosquito) is incorrect because mosquitoes transmit diseases like malaria (caused by Plasmodium), dengue, and chikungunya, but not sleeping sickness. Option 2 (House fly) is incorrect as house flies are mechanical vectors for diseases like typhoid and cholera but do not transmit trypanosomes. Option 3 (Sand Fly) is incorrect because sand flies transmit leishmaniasis (caused by Leishmaniaparasites), not African trypanosomiasis.

q: Rana Tigrina is the scientific name of which animal?
qs.e: The question tests knowledge of binomial nomenclature in zoology. Rana tigrina is the scientific name for the Asian frog, specifically the Indian bullfrog. In binomial nomenclature, the first part (Rana) represents the genus (capitalized), and the second part (tigrina) represents the species (lowercase). This naming system was established by Carolus Linnaeus. Option 1 (Tiger) is incorrect because its scientific name is Panthera tigris. Option 2 (Wolf) is incorrect as its scientific name is Canis lupus. Option 3 (Leopard) is incorrect with the scientific name Panthera pardus. Only option 4 correctly identifies Rana tigrina as an Asian frog species.

☛ The Indian bullfrog (Rana tigrina) is found in South and Southeast Asia.

☛ The genus name can be abbreviated after first use (e.g., R. tigrina).
☛ Rana is a genus of true frogs in the family Ranidae. Important One-liners for Upcoming Exams:

☛ What does 'Rana' represent in Rana tigrina? → Genus name
☛ Which animal has the scientific name Canis lupus? → Wolf
☛ How should scientific names be written? → Italicized with genus capitalized

q: Which of the following is a breed of milch animals?
qs.e: The question asks about breeds of milch animals (dairy cattle). Saheehwal is a well-known Indian dairy cattle breed, primarily reared for milk production in Punjab and Haryana. Nagori is a draught breed from Rajasthan, valued for pulling carts and ploughing. Harda Wadi is not a recognized cattle breed; it appears to be a distractor. q: Which of the following is an example of ectoparasite?
qs.e: Ectoparasites are organisms that live on the external surface of their host, deriving nutrition without entering the host's body. Mosquitoes (family Culicidae) are classic ectoparasites as they land on the skin, pierce it with their proboscis to feed on blood, and then leave. In contrast, tapeworms (Taenia solium) and hookworms (Ancylostoma duodenale) are endoparasites that live inside the host's intestines. Bacteria are microorganisms that can be parasitic but are not classified as ectoparasites; they typically infect internally or colonize surfaces without the specific host-attachment behavior of ectoparasites. Thus, only mosquitoes fit the ectoparasite definition.

☛ Malaria is transmitted by female Anophelesmosquitoes, while dengue is spread by Aedes aegypti.

☛ Parasites often show high host specificity and adaptations like reduced digestive systems.
☛ Vector-borne diseases involve ectoparasites transmitting pathogens between hosts. Important One-liners for Upcoming Exams:

☛ Which mosquito transmits malaria? → Female Anophelesmosquito.
☛ Example of an endoparasite? → Tapeworm (Taenia solium).
☛ Disease caused by Plasmodium ? → Malaria.
☛ What is a vector in biology? → An organism that transmits pathogens (e.g., mosquito for dengue).

q: The study of birds is called ________.
qs.e: The study of birds is called Ornithology. This branch of zoology focuses on the classification, behavior, physiology, ecology, and conservation of birds. Herpetology is incorrect because it deals with the study of reptiles and amphibians. Anthropology is wrong as it is the study of humans, their societies, and cultures. Ophthalmology is incorrect since it is the medical specialty concerned with the diagnosis and treatment of eye disorders. Ornithology specifically examines avian species, including their anatomy, migration patterns, and evolutionary history.
qs.kf:

q: Which of the following is a host in the life cycle of tape worm?
qs.e: The tapeworm Taenia solium (pork tapeworm) has a complex life cycle involving two hosts. The primary host is humans, where the adult worm resides in the small intestine and produces eggs. The intermediate host is the pig, where eggs develop into larvae (cysticerci) in muscle tissues. When humans consume undercooked pork containing cysticerci, they become infected. Option 1 (Pig) is correct as it serves as the intermediate host. Option 2 (Monkey) is incorrect—monkeys are not typical hosts for Taenia solium. Option 3 (Fish) is incorrect—fish are hosts for other tapeworms like Diphyllobothrium latum. Option 4 (Rabbit) is incorrect—rabbits are not natural hosts for common human tapeworms.
qs.kf:
☛ Taenia saginata (beef tapeworm) uses cattle as intermediate host and humans as definitive host.
☛ Tapeworms lack a digestive system—they absorb nutrients directly through their body surface.
☛ The scolex (head) has hooks and suckers for attachment to intestinal wall.
☛ Infection from Taenia soliumcan cause cysticercosis if eggs are ingested by humans.
☛ Proper cooking of meat (above 60°C) kills tapeworm larvae. Important One-liners for Upcoming Exams:
☛ Which tapeworm causes cysticercosis in humans? → Taenia solium
☛ What is the intermediate host for Taenia saginata ? → Cattle
☛ Where does adult tapeworm reside in humans? → Small intestine
☛ How do tapeworms obtain nutrition? → Absorption through body surface
☛ Which organ is affected in neurocysticercosis? → Brain

q: Which of the following is NOT an agent of dispersal of seeds?
qs.e: Seed dispersal is the movement or transport of seeds away from the parent plant to ensure germination and reduce competition. Agents of dispersal include wind (anemochory), water (hydrochory), and animals (zoochory). Wind disperses lightweight seeds with wings or hairs (e.g., dandelion). Water disperses buoyant seeds (e.g., coconut). Animals disperse seeds through ingestion and excretion (endozoochory) or attachment to fur (epizoochory). Sunlight is NOT an agent of dispersal; it is essential for photosynthesis and germination but does not physically move seeds. Thus, option 2 is correct because sunlight aids growth but not dispersal, while wind, animals, and water are direct dispersal agents.
qs.kf:
☛ Anemochory (wind dispersal) often involves seeds with parachutes (e.g., Taraxacum officinale- dandelion).
☛ Hydrochory (water dispersal) is common in aquatic plants like coconut (Cocos nucifera).
☛ Zoochory (animal dispersal) includes birds eating fruits and excreting seeds (e.g., figs by Ficusspecies).
☛ Some plants use explosive mechanisms (autochory) where fruits burst to scatter seeds (e.g., Impatiens).
☛ Dispersal increases genetic diversity and helps plants colonize new habitats, preventing overcrowding. Important One-liners for Upcoming Exams:
☛ What is seed dispersal by wind called? → Anemochory
☛ Which plant has water-dispersed seeds? → Coconut (Cocos nucifera)
☛ What is endozoochory? → Seed dispersal through animal ingestion and excretion
☛ Name a plant with explosive seed dispersal. → Balsam (Impatiens)
☛ Why is seed dispersal important? → Reduces competition and aids in colonization

q: Which of the following unicellular organism change their shape?
qs.e: The correct answer is Amoeba because it is a unicellular organism that exhibits amoeboid movement through the formation of temporary cytoplasmic extensions called pseudopodia (false feet). This allows it to change shape constantly for locomotion and feeding. Paramoecium (option 3) moves using hair-like structures called cilia and maintains a fixed slipper shape. Yeast (option 1) is a unicellular fungus with a rigid cell wall that maintains a spherical or oval shape.
